steps: Slope is how steep a line is

brief.title: The part under the square root
steps: A curve and a line
A quadratic draws a U shape. Solving it means asking where that U cuts the flat line at zero. Look at the picture: it can cut twice, touch once, or miss completely.
One number decides which
Inside the quadratic formula there is a square root. The stuff under that root is called the discriminant, and its SIGN alone tells you which of the three pictures you have.
Reading the sign
Positive means the root is a real number you can add and subtract: two answers. Zero means adding and subtracting nothing: one answer. Negative means no real root at all: the curve misses.
Why it is worth a look first
You can throw out wrong answer choices before doing any arithmetic, just from that one sign.

brief.title: Getting the unknown down from the exponent
steps: The unknown is out of reach
When x sits up in the exponent, nothing you do with plus, minus, times or divide will bring it down. You need the tool that is built to undo an exponent.
A log undoes its own base
ln and e cancel each other exactly. So do log and 10. Take the log of both sides and whatever was up in the exponent lands on the ground as an ordinary multiplier.
Clear the front first
If something is multiplying the exponential, divide it away BEFORE you take the log. Take the log too early and you have the log of a product instead of a clean exponent.
What is left is easy
After the log, the equation is a straight line in x. Divide and you are done.

rule-or-trap.title: Rule or Trap
rule-or-trap.closing: Products, quotients and powers have rules. A sum inside a log does not, and no amount of algebra will give it one. Using the rules on a real problem is still desk work.

brief.title: What a log is, and the rule that does not exist
steps: A log asks how many times
Three 2s multiplied together make 8. So the log of 8, in base 2, is 3. That is all a logarithm is: how many copies of the base you had to multiply.
Multiplying inside adds outside
Four 2s times three more 2s is seven 2s. Since the log just counts the copies, a product inside a log becomes a SUM outside it. A divide becomes a subtract, for the same reason.
A power drops to the front
A number raised to a power is that many copies of the copies, so the power simply comes down and multiplies.
There is no rule for a plus inside
Adding two numbers inside a log tells you nothing about the copies. Splitting one is the cheapest way to lose a mark on this topic.

People multiply the separate log VALUES together. The rule multiplies what is inside, never the answers.

brief.title: The three ratios, and picking one
steps: Same shape, same ratios
Every right triangle with the same angle has sides in the same proportions, however big it is drawn. Those fixed proportions are what sine, cosine and tangent are.
Three pairings, three names

The side the angle leans on takes cosine
Cosine goes with the adjacent side, the one the angle is measured from. So if the angle is measured up from the ground, the along-the-ground piece is the cosine one.
Measure from upright and they swap
Look at the second picture. Nothing about the push changed, only where the angle was measured from. Now the across piece takes sine.
So read the drawing, not the habit

which-law.title: Which Law
which-law.closing: A side with its opposite angle means Sines. Two sides with the angle between them, or all three sides, means Cosines. Choosing the way in is the part worth doing on a phone.

brief.title: Which law, and when
brief.lesson: Law of Sines & Law of Cosines
steps: No square corner, no SOH CAH TOA
A triangle with no right angle has no hypotenuse, so the three ratios have nothing to hang on. Two other relations hold in EVERY triangle instead.
Sines: a side paired with its own angle
Each side sits over the sine of the angle facing it, and all three of those fractions are equal. So one matched pair sets the scale for the whole triangle.
Cosines: nothing is paired
It is the Pythagorean theorem with a correction subtracted. Use it when you have two sides and the angle squeezed between them, or all three sides and no angle.
The one question to ask
Do I have a side together with the angle opposite it? Yes means sines. No means cosines.

brief.lesson: Law of Sines & Law of Cosines
steps: Cosine slides from plus one to minus one
At a tiny angle cosine is nearly 1. At a square corner it is exactly 0. Past that it goes negative and keeps falling. The sign is a message about how open the angle is.
When the top goes negative
Rearranged for an angle, the formula puts the side facing that angle on top with a minus in front. If that side squared beats the other two put together, the top is negative.
So the angle is past square
A negative cosine means an obtuse angle. It is not a mistake and it is not a sign error to fix.
Nothing needs subtracting from 180
The inverse cosine button already hands back the obtuse angle. "Correcting" it is how people turn a right answer into a wrong one.

walk-the-circle.title: Walk the Circle
walk-the-circle.closing: Cosine is the across, sine is the up, and the quadrant decides the signs. Knowing where a point sits is what makes the exact values worth memorising.

brief.title: Across is cosine, up is sine
steps: Walk round a circle of radius one
Start at the right-hand edge and sweep round anticlockwise. Wherever you stop, you are some distance across and some distance up.
Those two distances have names
How far ACROSS is the cosine of the angle. How far UP is the sine. That is the whole definition, and every other fact follows from it.
Which is why they are easy to swap
At 30 degrees you are far across and only a little up. At 60 it is the other way. Swapping the two swaps the angle.
Learn one quarter only
The other three quarters are mirrors of the first. Get the first quarter cold and you have the whole circle.

quadrant-signs.closing: The identity gives you the size, the quadrant gives you the sign. Forgetting the second half is how a right answer turns into a wrong one.

brief.title: The quarter you are in puts the sign back
steps: Squaring throws the sign away
Minus three squared and plus three squared are both nine. So any formula that goes through a square can only ever hand you back the SIZE of an answer, never whether it is plus or minus.
The circle remembers it
Across is positive to the right and negative to the left. Up is positive above the middle and negative below. Look at which quarter the angle lands in and both signs are decided.
So cosine and sine each have two good quarters
Cosine is positive on the right half, quarters one and four. Sine is positive on the top half, quarters one and two.
Stopping too early is the mistake
Getting the size from the identity and never checking the quarter gets you the right number with the wrong sign.

steps: There is a triangle inside the circle
Drop a line straight down from the point on the circle. You get a right triangle whose short sides are cosine and sine, and whose long side is the radius, which is 1.
So Pythagoras gives it to you free
Short side squared plus short side squared equals long side squared. That is sine squared plus cosine squared equals one. It is not a new fact, it is the triangle.
Doubling an angle is not doubling its sine
Turn twice as far and you do not get twice as high. sin of 2 theta needs BOTH functions and a 2 in front.
And the cosine one is a difference
cos of 2 theta is cosine squared MINUS sine squared, in that order. Flipping the order flips the sign of your answer.

Every circle is fixed by two things: where its middle sits, and how far it reaches out. Standard form hands you both with no work at all.
The sign flips
Whatever is inside a bracket, the center is the OPPOSITE. So x minus 2 means the center is 2 to the right, and y plus 3 means 3 BELOW the middle. It catches people every time.
The number on the right is squared
It is the radius times itself, not the radius. A 64 on the right means a reach of 8. Take the square root before you draw anything.

Look at the equation and ask a single question first: is x squared there, is y squared there, or only one of them?
Only one square is a parabola
One squared term and one plain one draws a U. The sign in front of the square decides whether the U opens up or down.
Both squares, same number, is a circle
If x squared and y squared carry exactly the same coefficient, every direction reaches the same distance. That is a circle.
Both squares, different numbers, is an ellipse
Different denominators stretch it one way. The BIGGER denominator sits under the long direction.

Look at the picture: a bracket raised to a power, with 3x plus 5 living inside it. Two layers, like a box in a box.
Peel the outside first
Treat the whole inside as one lump and differentiate the outer layer normally. Power 4 becomes 4 times power 3, with the lump untouched.
Then pay for the inside
The inside is changing too, three times as fast as x. So multiply by that 3. It goes OUTSIDE as a factor and never moves into the bracket.
It is nearly always there
Almost every derivative on this exam has an inside. The missing inner factor is the most common wrong answer there is.

steps: A square with a strip stuck on
Picture x squared as a real square, and the plain x term as a strip laid along its edge. Together they are ALMOST a bigger square, but a little corner is missing.
Cut the strip in half
Split the strip and lay half along the top and half down the side. Now the only thing stopping it from being a perfect square is one small corner block.
That corner is what you add
Its size is half the x number, squared. Add it and the left side folds neatly into one bracket squared.
Add it to BOTH sides
Adding it only on the left quietly changes the equation, and the radius you read off at the end comes out wrong.

sign-the-bend.title: Sign the Bend
sign-the-bend.closing: An inflection point needs the second derivative to be zero AND to change sign through it. Where the bend never changes there is no inflection point, however many flat spots the curve has.

brief.title: Smiles, frowns, and the flip
steps: Bend is not slope
A road can be going uphill and still be flattening out. Slope is which way you are heading. Bend is whether the road is curving toward the sky or toward the ground.
Smile up, frown down
The second derivative measures bend. Positive draws a smile, which would hold water. Negative draws a frown, which would spill it.
An inflection point is where it flips
It is the spot where a frown becomes a smile. Look at the picture: the curve is still climbing right through it, so nothing about the slope marks it.
Reaching zero is not enough
The second derivative must hit zero AND come out the other side with the OPPOSITE sign. A flat moment that goes back the way it came is not an inflection point.

slide-to-flat.title: Slide to the Flat Spot
slide-to-flat.closing: Maximum and minimum both sit where the slope is zero. Which one you are standing on is decided by the way the curve bends, not by the flat spot itself. Solving for it belongs on paper.

So the first move is always the same
Differentiate and set that equal to zero. Solving it gives you every place the curve levels off.
Flat alone does not say which
Zero slope happens at hilltops AND valley bottoms. You have found the places, not the kind.
The second derivative tells you the kind
Negative means the curve frowns, so you are on a hilltop. Positive means it smiles, so you are in a valley. A curve often has both.

which-way-simpler.title: Which Way Gets Simpler
which-way-simpler.closing: By parts trades one integral for another. The choice of u is right when the trade leaves you better off, which is all LIATE is telling you. Carrying it out belongs on paper.

brief.title: By parts, and which one is u
steps: It is a trade, not a solution
By parts swaps the integral you have for a different one. It is only worth doing if the new one is easier than the old one.
What decides that is your choice of u
Whatever you call u gets DIFFERENTIATED. Whatever is left gets integrated. So put the thing that gets simpler when you differentiate it in the u slot.
LIATE is that list, in order
Logs, Inverse trig, Algebra, Trig, Exponential. Whichever of your two pieces sits higher up the list becomes u.
Why that order
A log or a plain x collapses when you differentiate it. A sine or an e to the x never gets any simpler, so it goes in the other slot.

next-line.title: Which Line Comes Next
next-line.closing: Differentiate the top on its own and the bottom on its own. The quotient rule is for the derivative of a fraction; this is the limit of one, and they are not the same job.

brief.title: Top and bottom, separately
steps: Two different jobs, two different rules
The quotient rule finds the slope OF a fraction. This rule finds the limit of one. They look alike on the page and they give different answers.
Differentiate each one on its own
Slope of the top, written on top. Slope of the bottom, written underneath. Look at the picture: two separate arrows straight across.
Nothing multiplies, nothing is squared
There is no product term and no squared denominator. If either appears in your working you have reached for the wrong rule.
spoken: slope of the top over slope of the bottom
What the quotient rule does, which is not this
the one with a product and a squared bottom

picture.caption: top on its own, bottom on its own. Nothing multiplies and nothing is squared

ops.t: not the quotient rule: nothing squared

rounds.why: Top alone, bottom alone. The first line is the quotient rule, which is for differentiating a fraction, not for taking the limit of one. The third left the bottom untouched.

both-sides.title: Both Sides
both-sides.closing: A number over zero blows up, and which way it blows up depends on the side you came from. The two-sided limit exists only when the two directions agree.

brief.title: Both sides have to agree
steps: When the bottom goes to zero
A number divided by something tiny is enormous. So if the top settles on anything other than zero and the bottom vanishes, the fraction blows up.
Which way it blows up depends on the sign
A tiny positive bottom sends it up. A tiny negative bottom sends it down. And the sign can be different on the two sides of the point.
Both sides up: that is the limit
Left branch and right branch both shoot to the sky, so the answer is plus infinity.
One up and one down: no limit
The two sides disagree, so there is no single value to approach. The answer is that the limit does not exist, NOT that it is infinite.
spoken: both branches go up, so plus infinity
one branch up and one down, so there is no limit

left.caption: both sides shoot up: the limit is that infinity

right.caption: one up, one down: there is no limit at all

rounds.why: One over a small positive number is large and positive; one over a small negative number is large and negative. The sides disagree, so there is no two-sided limit. Answering plus infinity here is the other half of the trap on this problem.

land-the-resultant.title: Land the Resultant
land-the-resultant.closing: Vectors add component by component, never length by length. Once the resultant is placed, its size is the square root of the squares, and that part belongs at a desk.

brief.title: Adding arrows, one direction at a time
steps: Lay them head to tail
Put the start of the second arrow on the tip of the first. The answer is the arrow from where you began to where you ended up.
In numbers, add the parts separately
All the across parts together, all the up parts together, signs kept. Never add the lengths.
Why lengths do not add
Two pulls of 500 only make 1000 if they point the same way. Point them at each other and they make nothing at all. The direction is doing half the work.
spoken: so much across, so much up, so much out
across with across, up with up

picture.caption: lay the second arrow on the tip of the first. The answer runs start to finish

rounds.why: Three across and four up lands at three across and four up. Adding the lengths would have given seven, and seven is the distance you would walk, not the distance you end up from the start.

screen.text: Two pulls on a pin. Where does the resultant end?

screen.mono: Tap the point where the arrows add up to.

rounds.why: Add the across parts, then the up parts, signs and all: five minus two is three, and three minus four is minus one. The minus signs are doing real work here, and dropping them is the whole mistake.

screen.text: Three forces on a gusset plate. Where does the resultant end?

screen.mono: Tap the point where the arrows add up to.

rounds.why: The second arrow comes back down while it goes across, so the resultant sits lower than either arrow reached on its own.

screen.text: Where does the resultant end?

screen.mono: Tap the point where the arrows add up to.

rounds.why: Minus three and minus one is minus four; two and minus five is minus three. Every component keeps its sign through the addition, whatever quadrant the answer ends up in.

screen.text: Both arrows head into the third quadrant. Where do they land?

screen.mono: Tap the point where the arrows add up to.

rounds.why: Straight back where it started. Two arrows of the same length can add to nothing at all, which is exactly what adding their lengths could never tell you.

screen.text: Where does the resultant end?

screen.mono: Tap the point where the arrows add up to.

rounds.why: One plus two minus four is minus one; minus two plus four plus one is three. The order you add them in does not matter, which is worth knowing when a free body diagram has six arrows on it.

screen.text: Three arrows. Where does the resultant end?

screen.mono: Tap the point where the arrows add up to.

stretch-it.title: Stretch It to Fit
stretch-it.closing: A direction and a size are two separate things. The unit vector carries the direction, the multiplier carries the size, and a negative one turns it around.

brief.title: Direction without size
steps: An arrow exactly one long
A unit vector points where you want and has a length of exactly 1. It carries a direction and nothing else.
Make one by dividing
Take any arrow and divide it by its own length. Everything about the direction survives; only the size is scaled away.
Then size it to whatever you need
A force of 200 along that line is just 200 times the unit vector, and every component falls straight out.
A negative turns it around
Multiplying by a negative number keeps the same line and points the arrow the other way.
spoken: the arrow, over how long it is
the far end take away the near end

picture.caption: the unit arrow is the first fifth of the same arrow. same line, same direction, length exactly one

rounds.why: This one is already unit length, so the multiplier IS the magnitude. Five times it gives three across and four up, which is a five long arrow.

screen.text: Make an arrow 5 long along this direction.

rounds.why: This arrow is already 5 long, so ten times it would be fifty. The multiplier is only the magnitude when the direction is unit length, and that is the entire reason for dividing by the length first.

screen.text: Make an arrow 10 long along this direction.

rounds.why: A negative component is not a shorter arrow, it is an arrow pointing down as it goes across. The length still comes out at one before scaling.

screen.text: Make an arrow 4 long along this direction.

rounds.why: A negative multiplier turns the arrow around and keeps it on the same line. Three long, pointing down.

screen.text: Make an arrow 3 long along this direction, pointing the OTHER way.

rounds.why: Five long again, so doubling gets you ten. Notice the direction is untouched by the scaling: only the size changed.

screen.text: Make an arrow 10 long along this direction.

rounds.why: Unit length, so five is the size, and the minus is what sends it the other way. This is how a force is written along a line when it pushes rather than pulls.

screen.text: Make an arrow 5 long along this direction, pointing the OTHER way.

reaches-further.title: Which Reaches Further
reaches-further.closing: Length is the square root of the squares, so it is never the components added up. Two arrows with nothing in common can be exactly the same length.

brief.title: A length is not a component
steps: The arrow is the long side of a triangle
Go 3 across and 4 up. The arrow joining start to finish is the hypotenuse of that right triangle, so its length is 5, not 7.
Square, add, then root
That is Pythagoras, and it works the same way with a third direction added on.
A component is only a shadow
It is how far the arrow got along ONE axis. It is allowed to be negative, because you can go backwards along an axis.
A length never is
How far something reached cannot be a negative number. If a length comes out negative, something upstream is wrong.
spoken: square each part, add them, take the root
two triangles that come up again and again

picture.caption: the arrow is the long side of a right triangle, so its length is never the two parts added

ops.t: square them, add, then take the root

rounds.why: Six beats four and four. Their parts add to eight against six, which is why counting the parts up is no use: the second arrow spends its length going two ways at once.

screen.text: Which arrow is longer? They can also be the same.

rounds.why: The same length exactly, and this is the three four five triangle doing it. One has parts adding to seven and the other to five, and they still reach the same distance.

screen.text: Which arrow is longer? They can also be the same.

rounds.why: Six straight down beats four and four, and the minus signs change nothing about that. A negative component points an arrow the other way, it never makes it shorter, because everything gets squared before it is added.

screen.text: Which arrow is longer? They can also be the same.

rounds.why: Three beats two and two, even though two and two add to more. Going diagonally costs you: the parts have to be squared, and squaring punishes splitting your length between two directions.

screen.text: Which arrow is longer? They can also be the same.

rounds.why: Five, straight up, beats three and three. Their parts add to five against six, so the count of parts and the actual distance disagree about which one wins.

screen.text: Which arrow is longer? They can also be the same.

rounds.why: The same again, both of them five, and neither of them anywhere near the first quadrant. Three four five is worth recognizing on sight in any direction, because this exam uses it constantly.

screen.text: Which arrow is longer? They can also be the same.

take-the-diagonal.title: Take the Diagonal
take-the-diagonal.closing: Matching components only, signs kept, and the result is a number. If your answer has an i or a j in it you have done the cross product instead.

brief.title: Matching components, and a number at the end
steps: Pair each part with its own partner
Across with across, up with up, signs kept. Never across with up: that is the other product wearing the wrong name.
Multiply the pairs, then add
Two multiplications and one addition in two dimensions, three and two in three. That is the whole calculation.
What comes out is a plain number
No direction, no arrow, no letters. If your answer still has an i or a j in it, you did the cross product instead.
spoken: multiply the matching parts and add them up
the answer is a plain number, with no direction

picture.caption: across pairs with across, up pairs with up. Multiply the pairs and add

ops.t: if an i or a j survives, you did the other product

rounds.why: Across with across, up with up. The minus on B stays: three times minus two is minus six, and minus six plus twenty is fourteen. The off-diagonal cells are the cross product asking to be let in.

screen.text: Every possible pairing is here. Tap the ones that belong in the dot product.

rounds.why: A zero component contributes nothing, but it still has to be paired with its own partner rather than skipped over. Everything here comes from the one cell that is not zero, and the answer is three.

screen.text: Every possible pairing is here. Tap the ones that belong in the dot product.

rounds.why: Two negatives multiply to a positive, so the second cell adds three rather than taking it away. Sign slips are the most common way this formula goes wrong.

screen.text: Every possible pairing is here. Tap the ones that belong in the dot product.

rounds.why: Three dimensions, three cells, still the diagonal. This is the joint and the member from the worked problem with the hundreds taken off. Six plus eighteen minus three is twenty one, and the k pairing is the only one that takes anything away.

screen.text: Every possible pairing is here. Tap the ones that belong in the dot product.

rounds.why: Four minus four is nothing, and the k pairing contributes nothing either, so the whole dot product is zero. That means these two are perpendicular, which is worth more than the number.

screen.text: Every possible pairing is here. Tap the ones that belong in the dot product.

rounds.why: Two of the three cells are zero and the answer comes from one pairing. Which is fine. What is not fine is pairing the five with the three because they are the only interesting numbers on screen.

screen.text: Every possible pairing is here. Tap the ones that belong in the dot product.

open-or-closed.title: Open or Closed
open-or-closed.closing: The sign of a dot product is the sign of the cosine, because the two lengths are always positive. Under ninety, positive. Over ninety, negative. Exactly ninety, zero, and that is the perpendicularity test.

brief.title: The sign is the angle
steps: The same number, told another way
The dot product also equals the two lengths multiplied together, times the cosine of the angle between the arrows.
Lengths are always positive
So the only thing in that product that can be negative is the cosine. The sign of a dot product IS the sign of the cosine.
Which reads the angle straight off
Positive means the arrows are closing, under a square corner. Negative means they are opening, past it. Zero means exactly square.
That zero is the quickest test there is
For the angle itself, rearrange and take the inverse cosine. And remember the cosine is not the angle.
spoken: the two lengths, times the cosine of the angle between
divide by both lengths, then undo the cosine
zero means the two are at a square corner

picture.caption: the sign of the answer is the sign of the cosine, and nothing else

ops.t: zero is the fastest square-corner test there is

rounds.why: They lean the same way, so the angle between them is under ninety and the cosine is positive. You never had to multiply anything to know the sign.

screen.text: Is the dot product of these two positive, zero, or negative?

rounds.why: A right angle, so the dot product is exactly zero. This is the perpendicularity test, and it is the fastest check for it there is: no lengths, no inverse cosine, just zero or not.

screen.text: Is the dot product of these two positive, zero, or negative?

rounds.why: More than ninety degrees apart, so the cosine is negative and so is the dot product. The arrows disagree about which way to go, and the sign says so.

screen.text: Is the dot product of these two positive, zero, or negative?

rounds.why: Both point into the left half, so they still lean the same way as each other and the answer is positive. Where the arrows sit on the page has nothing to do with it; the angle BETWEEN them is the whole story.

screen.text: Is the dot product of these two positive, zero, or negative?

rounds.why: Straight up against straight across is the easiest right angle to see, and zero is the answer. Notice the two arrows are nowhere near the same length, and it changed nothing.

screen.text: Is the dot product of these two positive, zero, or negative?

rounds.why: Just past ninety degrees, and past is enough. This is the one worth being careful with: it looks close, and the components decide it rather than the eye. Two minus fifteen is negative.

screen.text: Is the dot product of these two positive, zero, or negative?

shadow-falls.title: Where the Shadow Falls
shadow-falls.closing: The component of a force along a member is the dot product divided by the MEMBER length, never the force length, and never left undivided. Working the number out belongs at a desk.

brief.title: How much of a force lands on a member
steps: Think of a shadow
Shine a light straight down onto the member. The shadow the force casts along it is how much of that force the member actually feels.
Dot product, then divide by the MEMBER
The dot product gives the shadow multiplied by the member length. Divide by the member length to get the shadow on its own.
Dividing by the wrong one breaks it
Not dividing leaves you something that is not a force. Dividing by the force gives a number that has forgotten what it measured.
The sign still means something
Negative means the force runs back along the member instead of out along it.
spoken: the dot product, over the length of the direction
the force dotted with the unit arrow along the member

picture.caption: shine a light straight down on the member. The shadow is how much of the force lands on it

ops.t: divide by the length of the MEMBER, not the force

rounds.why: Along a horizontal member only the across part of the force does any work, so the shadow is 3. The up part contributes nothing to this member no matter how big it is.

screen.overline: HOW MUCH LANDS ON THE MEMBER

screen.text: Drop the force onto the member and tap the mark its shadow reaches.

screen.mono: The member runs along 1i + 0j, marked off in whole units.

rounds.why: The dot product with the raw member would be 15, and 15 is not a length anybody wants: it is the shadow times the member. Dividing by the member length of 5 leaves the shadow, which is 3.

screen.overline: HOW MUCH LANDS ON THE MEMBER

screen.text: Drop the force onto the member and tap the mark its shadow reaches.

screen.mono: The member runs along 3i + 4j, marked off in whole units.

rounds.why: Same member, a force straight up instead of straight across, and the shadow is 4. The member leans more up than across, so it catches more of this one.

screen.overline: HOW MUCH LANDS ON THE MEMBER

screen.text: Drop the force onto the member and tap the mark its shadow reaches.

screen.mono: The member runs along 3i + 4j, marked off in whole units.

rounds.why: Behind the joint. A projection is signed: negative means the force pushes back along the member rather than out along it, and dropping the sign turns a compression into a tension.

screen.overline: HOW MUCH LANDS ON THE MEMBER

screen.text: Drop the force onto the member and tap the mark its shadow reaches.

screen.mono: The member runs along 3i + 4j, marked off in whole units.

rounds.why: The force is square on to the member, so its shadow is nothing and the member carries none of it. This is the perpendicularity test arriving as a length rather than as a number.

screen.overline: HOW MUCH LANDS ON THE MEMBER

screen.text: Drop the force onto the member and tap the mark its shadow reaches.

screen.mono: The member runs along 4i - 3j, marked off in whole units.

rounds.why: Six along the member, out of a force that is a little over six long in total. Almost all of it lands on the member, because the two very nearly line up.

screen.overline: HOW MUCH LANDS ON THE MEMBER

screen.text: Drop the force onto the member and tap the mark its shadow reaches.

screen.mono: The member runs along 3i + 4j, marked off in whole units.

which-way-turns.title: Which Way Does It Turn
which-way-turns.closing: Sweep from the first arrow to the second: counterclockwise means the cross product comes out of the page, clockwise means it goes in, and two arrows on one line turn nothing. Swapping the order swaps the answer.

brief.title: Which way it turns, and why order matters
steps: This one gives back an arrow
Unlike the dot product, a cross product IS a vector. It points square to both of the arrows that made it.
Your right hand picks which way
Fingers along the first arrow, curl them toward the second, and your thumb points the answer. Sweeping anticlockwise brings it out of the page; clockwise sends it in.
So the order is not a detail
Swap the two arrows and the answer flips over completely. That is why a moment is r cross F, in that order, and never the other way.
Two arrows on one line give nothing
There is no turn to measure, so the answer is zero.
spoken: the arm crossed into the force, that way round
swapping them turns the answer round
no turn at all, so nothing

left.caption: sweeping this way brings the answer out of the page

right.caption: sweeping the other way sends it in

rounds.why: Sweep from r round to F the short way and it goes counterclockwise, so the moment points out of the page. That is the right-hand rule: fingers along r, curl to F, thumb comes at you.

screen.overline: SWEEP FROM THE FIRST TO THE SECOND

screen.text: A force pushes up at the end of a horizontal arm.

screen.mono: Which way does r cross F turn?

rounds.why: A downward pull on an arm reaching up and to the right turns it clockwise, into the page. This is the worked moment problem with the zeros left off.

screen.overline: SWEEP FROM THE FIRST TO THE SECOND

screen.text: A weight hangs off an arm that reaches out and up.

screen.mono: Which way does r cross F turn?

rounds.why: Same arrows, opposite answer. A cross product changes sign when you swap the order, which is why a moment is r cross F and never F cross r. Getting this backwards reverses every moment in the problem.

screen.overline: SWEEP FROM THE FIRST TO THE SECOND

screen.text: The same two arrows as the last round, crossed the other way round.

screen.mono: Which way does F cross r turn?

rounds.why: Up the post, then push to the right, and the post rotates clockwise about its base. Nothing here is in the first quadrant twice, and the rule still only cares about the sweep from the first to the second.

screen.overline: SWEEP FROM THE FIRST TO THE SECOND

screen.text: A horizontal push at the top of a vertical post.

screen.mono: Which way does r cross F turn?

rounds.why: No turn at all. A force pointing straight along the arm cannot rotate anything about the pivot, and the cross product of two arrows on the same line is zero. A vector crossed with itself is the same story.

screen.overline: SWEEP FROM THE FIRST TO THE SECOND

screen.text: The force runs straight along the arm.

screen.mono: Which way does r cross F turn?

rounds.why: Counterclockwise, so u cross v points out of the page. For an area this only decides the sign, and the area is the size of it either way. For a moment the sign is the answer.

screen.overline: SWEEP FROM THE FIRST TO THE SECOND

screen.text: Two edges of a plot, taken in the order they are written.

screen.mono: Which way does u cross v turn?

which-region.title: Which Region
which-region.closing: The cross product measures the parallelogram. A triangle is half of it, and the two lengths multiplied without the sine are a box that is too big. Which one you hand in is decided by the question, not the formula.

brief.title: The parallelogram, and half of it
steps: The size of a cross product is an area
Take the two arrows as two edges and slide them into a leaning box. The cross product gives exactly that area.
A triangle is half of it
A plot of land bounded by those same two edges is the other half cut off. So it takes a divide by two the formula will not remind you about.
The sine accounts for the lean
Just multiplying the two lengths would give the upright box round the whole thing. That is only right when the edges meet at a square corner.
spoken: the two lengths, times the sine of the angle between

left.caption: the cross product gives THIS area

right.caption: a triangle on the same two edges is half of it

rounds.why: The parallelogram, always. The two edges and their two copies close it up, and the cross product measures exactly that much ground.

screen.overline: THE SAME TWO EDGES, THREE WAYS

screen.text: The magnitude of the cross product is the area of which region?

rounds.why: Half the parallelogram, which is the triangle. This is the whole trap on the surveying problem: the cross product hands you twice the plot and it is on you to halve it.

screen.overline: THE SAME TWO EDGES, THREE WAYS

screen.text: A plot is bounded by these two edges and the line joining them. Which region do you hand in?

rounds.why: That expression IS the magnitude of the cross product, written the other way round, so it is the parallelogram again. The sine is what takes the lean into account.

screen.overline: THE SAME TWO EDGES, THREE WAYS

screen.text: Which region has area equal to the two lengths times the sine of the angle between them?

rounds.why: A box, and only a box. Dropping the sine pretends the two edges meet at a right angle, and it overstates the area of every plot that is not actually square.

screen.overline: THE SAME TWO EDGES, THREE WAYS

screen.text: Which region would the two lengths multiplied together give, with no sine anywhere?

rounds.why: Four across crossed with two across and three up gives twelve, and twelve is the parallelogram. The plot on the exam paper was six.

screen.overline: THE SAME TWO EDGES, THREE WAYS

screen.text: These edges span 12 square meters between them. Which region is that?

rounds.why: The triangle, and the number the question actually wanted. Twelve is sitting right there in the working, which is why it is the wrong answer people pick.

screen.overline: THE SAME TWO EDGES, THREE WAYS

screen.text: Same two edges. Which region is 6 square meters?

fix-the-sign.title: Fix the Sign
fix-the-sign.closing: Plus, minus, plus across the three components. The middle one is subtracted every single time, and a minus in front of a negative bracket is where the moments go backwards.

brief.title: Plus, minus, plus
steps: Cover one column at a time
Write the grid: i, j and k across the top, then each arrow on its own row. Cover the i column and two columns are left over. Those two make the i term. Do the same for j and for k.
The middle one had to jump a gap
Look at what survives each time. Covering i leaves columns 2 and 3, side by side. Covering k leaves 1 and 2, side by side. Covering j leaves 1 and 3, with a column jumped between them.
That jump is what the minus pays for
The j term is the only one out of step, so it is the only one taken away. Plus, minus, plus. Get it backwards and the moment points the wrong way.
The answer is still a vector
If the question asked for a size, take the magnitude afterwards.
spoken: Cover a column, keep the rest
cover the i column and the two that are left make this piece

picture.caption: cover one column at a time. the middle one is the only one whose two leftover columns are not neighbors

ops.t: the odd one out is the one that gets the minus

rounds.why: The middle term is SUBTRACTED. It should read minus the bracket, which turns minus fifteen into plus fifteen. A minus in front of a negative is where this goes wrong, and it flips the whole moment.

screen.text: One line may have the wrong sign. Tap it, or say the whole thing is right.

rounds.why: Plus, minus, plus, and the minus did its job. The moment points up and back, and this is the worked answer with the fifty scaled down to a five.

screen.text: One line may have the wrong sign. Tap it, or say the whole thing is right.

rounds.why: One times one is a positive one, and the k term is added, so it is plus one. Minus one would be j crossed with i, the other way round. This is the one worth knowing on sight: i cross j is k.

rounds.why: The i bracket is all zeros, so the i component is nothing. The 12 belongs to k and has been copied into the wrong line. Both edges lie flat, so the answer can only point out of the page.

copy-it-down.title: Copy It Down
copy-it-down.closing: A plain reference moves with the copy and a dollar sign pins whatever comes straight after it. Nothing tells you which you need except knowing what has to stay put, and the rate is almost always the thing that stays put.

brief.title: What moves when you copy
steps: A plain reference slides
Write B1 in a cell and copy the formula one row down. It quietly becomes B2. Copy it across and it becomes C1. It shifts by however far you moved it.
A dollar sign nails it down
Whatever comes straight after a dollar sign cannot move. So B$1 always points at row 1, and $B1 always points at column B.
Two dollar signs pin it completely
A fixed number, like an interest rate in one cell, wants both.
The mistake it causes
A missing dollar sign lets the rate drift down the column. The first row is right and every row under it is quietly wrong.

picture.caption: copy a formula down and a plain reference slides with it. A dollar sign nails it down

ops.t: the missing dollar sign is the commonest sheet mistake

rounds.why: Down one row. A1 is relative so it walks down to A2, and the dollar signs hold B1 exactly where it is. This is the unit price pattern: a column of quantities times one fixed rate.

screen.overline: WHERE DOES IT POINT AFTER THE COPY

screen.text: This formula is copied from C1 to C2. Tap the cells the copy reads.

rounds.why: Down two rows this time, so the relative half walks two rows with it. The locked half does not care how far the copy went.

screen.overline: WHERE DOES IT POINT AFTER THE COPY

screen.text: This formula is copied from C1 to C3. Tap the cells the copy reads.

rounds.why: No dollar signs anywhere, so both halves move. This is the row that goes wrong when somebody forgets to lock the rate: every line below the first quietly multiplies by the wrong cell.

screen.overline: WHERE DOES IT POINT AFTER THE COPY

screen.text: This formula is copied from C1 to C2. Tap the cells the copy reads.

rounds.why: One dollar sign each, and they lock different things. The A keeps its column and moves down a row; the B keeps its row and moves across a column. A dollar sign locks only what comes straight after it.

screen.overline: WHERE DOES IT POINT AFTER THE COPY

screen.text: This formula is copied from C2 to D3. Tap the cells the copy reads.

rounds.why: Across one column, not down. Fully locked stays at A1, and B2 slides sideways to C2. Copying across moves the letters; copying down moves the numbers.

rounds.why: Two references into the same column, and only one of them moves. The row lock on the first one is doing all the work, which is what a running total against a fixed header looks like.

happens-first.title: Which Happens First
happens-first.closing: Brackets, then powers, then times and divide, then plus and minus, and same rank goes left to right. A spreadsheet never reads a formula the way you read a sentence.

brief.title: A sheet does not read left to right
steps: There is an order, and it is not reading order
Brackets first. Then powers. Then multiply and divide. Then add and subtract. Anything of equal rank runs left to right.
So the times jumps the queue
Two plus three times four is 14, not 20, however it reads on the page. The multiply happens before the add.
Brackets are the only override
Put the add in brackets and it goes first. Nothing else changes the order.
spoken: three fours are twelve, then add two

picture.caption: the same four symbols, read two ways. Only brackets change the order

rounds.why: Multiplication outranks addition, so three times four happens before anything is added to it. Reading left to right would give twenty; the sheet gives fourteen.

screen.text: Tap the part of this formula the spreadsheet works out first.

rounds.why: Division outranks addition just as multiplication does. This is the exact formula the lesson warns about: it does not add A1 and A2 and then divide, it divides first.

screen.text: Tap the part of this formula the spreadsheet works out first.

rounds.why: Brackets beat everything. They are how you force the addition to happen first, and without them the same three cells give a different number.

screen.text: Tap the part of this formula the spreadsheet works out first.

rounds.why: The power goes before the multiply. Order of operations runs brackets, then powers, then times and divide, then plus and minus.

screen.text: Tap the part of this formula the spreadsheet works out first.

rounds.why: Divide and multiply are the same rank, so nothing outranks anything and it goes left to right. The division is simply written first.

screen.text: Tap the part of this formula the spreadsheet works out first.

rounds.why: Plus and minus are also the same rank, so again it is left to right. Doing the addition first here would change the answer, which is why the rank AND the reading order both matter.

what-shows.title: What Does the Cell Show
what-shows.closing: A cell holds a formula and shows a result. IF returns one branch or the other and never a 1, COUNT ignores anything that is not a number, and a colon always means every cell in between.

brief.title: What the common functions hand back
steps: The simple ones do what they say
SUM adds a range up. AVERAGE takes its mean. MAX and MIN pull the biggest and the smallest out of it.
COUNT only counts numbers
Look at the picture: five cells, but two of them hold words. COUNT sees three. Text inside the range is skipped in silence.
A colon means everything between
B1 colon B3 is B1, B2 and B3, not just the two ends.
IF hands back a value, not a true
It checks the test, then gives you the second thing when the test passes and the third when it fails. It never returns a 1.
spoken: add up every cell from B1 to B3
if the test passes give the middle one, otherwise the last one

picture.caption: five cells, but COUNT only sees the numbers in them

ops.t: text in the range is skipped

rounds.why: Twelve is at least ten, so the test passes and the middle argument is what comes back: twelve doubled. Seventeen is the other branch, and the 1 is what you get by treating TRUE as a number.

rounds.why: A colon means a range, and SUM adds everything in it. The 3 is what COUNT would give you and the 30 is the average.

rounds.why: The same range, the arithmetic mean instead of the total. Ninety is the sum sitting right beside it, which is why the two get handed in for each other.

screen.text: Cell C2 holds this. What does it show?

rounds.why: COUNT counts NUMBERS. The cell holding text is in the range and is not counted, so the answer is three and not four. Fifteen is what SUM would have given.

fill-the-trace.title: Fill the Trace
fill-the-trace.closing: A loop from one to four runs four times, both ends included, and the way to be sure is to write the rows out. The answer is the last row, not the number of rows.

brief.title: Trace it, one row per pass
steps: Only three things ever happen
Steps in order, a choice between paths, and a repeat. Every routine on this exam is built out of those three.
Write a table, not a guess
Put the variables in columns and fill in one row for every pass. Trying to hold the whole loop in your head is where it goes wrong.
A counted loop includes both ends
FOR i = 1 TO 4 runs FOUR times, not three. Both ends are in.
The answer is the last row
It is almost never the number of rows. Look at what the variable holds at the end, not at how many times you went round.
spoken: one, two, three, four: both ends counted
the running total after each pass

picture.caption: one row per pass. The answer is usually the last row, not how many rows there are

ops.t: FOR i = 1 TO 4 runs four times

rounds.why: Four passes, because the endpoints are both included. Stopping at three leaves you with six, which is the off-by-one the lesson warns about, and fifteen is a pass too many.

screen.text: Fill in what total holds after each pass.

rounds.why: The same four passes with twice as much added each time, so every row is double the first round. The shape of the trace never changes, only what goes into it.

screen.text: Fill in what total holds after each pass.

rounds.why: A product accumulator, and it has to start at one. Starting a product at zero would leave it at zero forever, which is worth noticing before you write your own.

screen.text: Fill in what p holds after each pass.

rounds.why: Three passes, going down instead of up. The starting value is not always zero and the loop does not care which way the numbers move.

screen.text: Fill in what total holds after each pass.

rounds.why: This one counts passes rather than adding them up, and it lands on four. Four is how many times the loop ran; fourteen is what the values would have added to. Those are different questions.

screen.text: Fill in what count holds after each pass.

rounds.why: Starting at zero still gives four passes, because both ends are included. The first pass adds nothing at all, which makes the row easy to skip and the count easy to get wrong.

first-true-wins.title: First True Wins
first-true-wins.closing: Conditions are read from the top and the chain stops at the first one that holds. A later test that would also have been true never gets its turn, and the closing ELSE only runs when every test above it has failed.

brief.title: The first true condition wins
steps: Checked from the top down
The machine tries each test in order and stops dead at the first one that holds. Everything below is skipped.
Even a later test that is also true
A chain is not a search for the best match. Look at the picture: x is 7, which passes two of the tests, and only the first one runs.
ELSE is the catch-all
It only runs when every test above it has failed. Reading the whole chain first and picking the best fit is how people land here by mistake.
Watch the boundary
Greater than leaves the number itself out. Greater than or equal to takes it in.
spoken: top to bottom, stopping at the first one that holds
the first test it passes, and no other

picture.caption: checked from the top down, and it stops dead at the first one that holds

ops.t: a later test that is also true never gets a turn

rounds.why: Seven is not over ten, so the first test fails, but seven is over five, so the second one holds and the chain stops there. The closing ELSE never gets looked at.

screen.overline: TOP TO BOTTOM, STOP AT THE FIRST

screen.text: Tap the branch that actually runs.

rounds.why: Ten is not greater than ten. A strict greater than excludes the number itself, so the first test fails on the boundary and the second one picks it up.

screen.overline: TOP TO BOTTOM, STOP AT THE FIRST

screen.text: Tap the branch that actually runs.

rounds.why: Both tests fail this time, so the closing ELSE is what runs. It is the right answer here and the wrong one everywhere else in this set, which is exactly why it gets picked too often.

screen.overline: TOP TO BOTTOM, STOP AT THE FIRST

screen.text: Tap the branch that actually runs.

rounds.why: Forty is at least forty, so the second test holds. The third one would ALSO have held, and it never runs, because the chain stops at the first thing that is true rather than the best fit.

screen.overline: TOP TO BOTTOM, STOP AT THE FIRST

screen.text: Tap the branch that actually runs.

rounds.why: Five is not under zero and not over five, so both tests fail and the closing ELSE runs. Sitting exactly on a strict boundary means neither side claims you.

screen.overline: TOP TO BOTTOM, STOP AT THE FIRST

rounds.why: Twelve is not at least twenty, and it is exactly twelve, so the second test holds on its boundary. A chain like this is how a schedule of sizes gets written, and getting the boundary wrong specifies the wrong bar.

where-it-stops.title: Where It Stops
where-it-stops.closing: The condition is checked before the body, so the value left in the variable is the one that broke it. Nothing is capped at the limit, and a loop whose condition fails at the first look never runs at all.

brief.title: A WHILE checks before it acts
steps: The test comes first, every time
Including the very first pass. If the condition is already false when the loop is reached, the body never runs at all.
So the value left behind broke the test
Doubling while under 100 does not stop at 64. It doubles to 128, the test fails, and 128 is what is left in the variable.
Nothing is capped at the limit
The number in the condition is a gate to pass through, not a ceiling to stop at.
spoken: each pass doubles, and the last one goes over
the value that failed the test, not the last one that passed

picture.caption: the test runs BEFORE each pass, so the value left behind is the one that broke it

ops.t: the one left behind is 128, not 64
nothing is capped at the number in the test

rounds.why: At 64 the condition still holds, so the body runs once more and doubles it to 128. Only then does the check fail. Sixty four is the last value that passed the test, not the value left behind.

screen.text: Tap the value left in the variable when the loop stops.

screen.v: EVERY VALUE IT TAKES

rounds.why: Tripling overshoots harder, and 81 is well past the fifty in the condition. Nothing caps a loop at its limit; the limit only decides when to stop going round.

screen.text: Tap the value left in the variable when the loop stops.

screen.v: EVERY VALUE IT TAKES

rounds.why: Running down instead of up, and it undershoots for the same reason: at 8 the condition holds, so it halves once more to 4 and only then gives up.

screen.text: Tap the value left in the variable when the loop stops.

screen.v: EVERY VALUE IT TAKES

rounds.why: Adding rather than multiplying changes nothing about the rule. Eighteen passes the test, so six more go on, and 24 is what is left when the loop stops.

screen.v: EVERY VALUE IT TAKES

rounds.why: This condition allows the limit itself, but 32 is the last value under it either way and doubling takes you to 64. An "or equal to" changes which values pass, never what is left at the end.

screen.v: EVERY VALUE IT TAKES

rounds.why: The condition is checked BEFORE the body, and it fails on the very first look, so the body never runs once. The variable is left exactly as it started. A loop is allowed to do nothing.

follow-the-tangent.title: Follow the Tangent
follow-the-tangent.closing: One iteration slides down the tangent to the axis and stops there. It lands short of the root, on the far side of a flat slope, or exactly on it if the function was a line. Grinding out the arithmetic belongs at a desk.

brief.title: Slide down the tangent
steps: It is a picture before it is a formula
Stand on the curve at your guess. Follow the straight line that just touches it there, all the way down to the axis. Stand at that new spot and do it again.
That slide is what the formula does
Dividing the function by its slope is exactly how far along the tangent takes you.
Why it closes in so fast
Zoom in near a root and any smooth curve looks almost straight, so the tangent lands very close to the truth.
And why a flat slope ruins it
A nearly flat tangent runs a very long way before it meets the axis, and you land somewhere useless.
spoken: your guess, minus the height divided by the slope
height twelve, slope eight, so slide back one and a half

picture.caption: stand on the curve, slide down the tangent to the axis, and stand there instead

rounds.why: The tangent at 4 meets the axis at 2.5, and that is where one iteration leaves you. The root is at 2 and you are not there yet; one step of Newton gets you closer, not finished.

screen.text: Where does one step of Newton leave you?

rounds.why: Forty eight over sixteen is three, taken AWAY from eight. Eleven is what adding it gives, and it walks you away from the root instead of towards it.

screen.text: Where does one step of Newton leave you?

rounds.why: When the function IS a straight line, the tangent is the function, so one iteration lands exactly on the root. This is the best case Newton has and it is why the method converges so fast near a root, where every curve is nearly straight.

screen.text: Where does one step of Newton leave you?

rounds.why: Twenty seven over twelve is 2.25, so the tangent lands at 3.75 with the root at 3 still ahead. A second iteration from here would land much closer, which is what fast convergence looks like.

screen.text: Where does one step of Newton leave you?

rounds.why: Here the slope is only 1, so the tangent is nearly flat and it takes a very long walk to reach the axis. One step throws you from 0.5 all the way to 4.25, further from the root than you started. This is the divergence the lesson warns about, and a flat derivative is what causes it.

screen.text: Where does one step of Newton leave you?

rounds.why: Upside down, and nothing changes. The function and its slope are both negative now, and the two minus signs cancel in the division, so the step is the same size and the same direction as the first round.

screen.text: Where does one step of Newton leave you?

can-it-start.title: Can It Start Here
can-it-start.closing: Bisection needs the two ends on opposite sides of the axis and nothing else. A span can hold two roots and still fail the test, and a curve with no roots fails it everywhere.

brief.title: Opposite sides, then halve it
steps: It asks for one thing only
The curve below the axis at one end of your interval and above it at the other. Then it has to cross somewhere in between.
The test is a multiplication
Multiply the two end values. A negative answer means one was positive and one negative, which is exactly the sign change you need.
Then cut it in half, over and over
Check the middle, keep whichever half still has the sign change, repeat. The gap halves every time.
Same signs does not mean no root
It means this method cannot be STARTED there, which is a different thing. An interval holding two roots fails the test for that reason.
spoken: the two end values multiply to something negative
Then keep the half that still has it
whichever side of the middle still changes sign

picture.caption: one end below the axis, one end above. Somewhere between them it must cross

rounds.why: Only B has the curve below the axis at one end and above it at the other. A is entirely below and C entirely above, and neither of them has anywhere for a crossing to hide.

screen.text: Which span can bisection be started on?

screen.mono: f(x) = x squared minus 4

rounds.why: A holds BOTH roots, so the function comes back to the same side it started on and bisection cannot be started on it even though there are two crossings inside. B holds one crossing and has opposite signs, which is the whole requirement. C sits under the axis at both ends.

screen.text: Which span can bisection be started on?

screen.mono: f(x) = x squared minus 6x plus 8

rounds.why: C crosses from below to above, so it qualifies. A is above the axis at both ends and B is below at both ends, and being close to a root is not the same as having one bracketed.

screen.text: Which span can bisection be started on?

screen.mono: f(x) = x squared minus 6x plus 8

rounds.why: B, and the curve running downwards rather than upwards changes nothing: the test is opposite SIGNS, not which way the function is heading. The wide span holds both roots and comes back to the sign it started with.

screen.text: Which span can bisection be started on?

screen.mono: f(x) = 4 minus x squared

rounds.why: A brackets the crossing at minus two. This curve has three roots and the other two are nowhere near B or C, both of which sit entirely on one side of the axis. More roots does not mean more brackets.

screen.text: Which span can bisection be started on?

screen.mono: f(x) = x cubed minus 4x

rounds.why: None of them. This curve never touches the axis at all, so it has no root to bracket and no interval can be made to work. Bisection is not a method for finding roots that are not there.

screen.text: Which span can bisection be started on?

screen.mono: f(x) = x squared plus 1

which-method.title: Which Method
which-method.closing: Newton is fast and wants a derivative and a decent guess. Bisection is slow and wants nothing but a sign change. Knowing which one the situation allows is most of what this topic asks.

brief.title: Fast, or guaranteed
steps: Newton is fast and fussy
It wants the slope AND a guess that is already near the root. Give it a poor guess or a nearly flat slope and it can wander off or swing back and forth without ever settling.
Bisection is slow and reliable
No slope needed and no good guess needed. Just two ends with opposite signs. Once it has that, it cannot fail.
So the question is what you have
Not which method is cleverer. Read what the problem hands you and pick the one whose requirements are met.
spoken: the slope, and a starting guess near the answer
only two ends on opposite sides of the axis

picture.caption: what you have decides the method, not which one is cleverer

options: Newton, but it may not converge
rounds.why: This is exactly what Newton is for. Near a root every curve is nearly straight, which is why following the tangent gets so close so fast.

child.v: You have the derivative, and a starting guess you know sits close to the root. You want an answer in as few steps as possible.

c.v: Newton, but it may not converge
the tangent will not help here

options: Newton, but it may not converge
rounds.why: A sign change is the whole of what bisection asks for, and it does not want a derivative. It is slower, and it will get there.

child.v: All you know is that the function is above the axis at x = 1 and below it at x = 4. You do not have the derivative.

c.v: Newton, but it may not converge
the tangent will not help here

options: Newton, but it may not converge
rounds.why: An almost flat tangent takes an enormous walk to reach the axis, so the step is huge and lands nowhere useful. A derivative near zero is the named cause of Newton diverging.

child.v: You have the derivative, but the guess you were handed sits where the curve is almost flat.

c.v: Newton, but it may not converge
the tangent will not help here

options: Newton, but it may not converge
rounds.why: The tangent to a line is the line, so one iteration lands exactly on the root. This is the best Newton ever does, and it is the reason it behaves so well once it gets close.

child.v: The function is a straight line and you know its slope.

c.v: Newton, but it may not converge
the tangent will not help here

options: Newton, but it may not converge
rounds.why: A far guess is the other named cause. The tangent out there points somewhere unrelated to the root, so the method can wander off or swing back and forth without settling.

child.v: You have the derivative, but the only guess you have is a long way from the root, on a curve that bends about a good deal in between.

c.v: Newton, but it may not converge
the tangent will not help here

options: Newton, but it may not converge
rounds.why: Bisection is the one with a guarantee. As long as the interval brackets a sign change it cannot fail, and the price of that is halving the interval instead of leaping at the answer.

child.v: It has to converge. You can afford to wait, and you would rather not find out afterwards that it ran away.

c.v: Newton, but it may not converge
the tangent will not help here
